title: A Leader’s Relationship With Decisions
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that what matters most about a leader's decisions is not only their quality but the degree to which the leader owns them. It distinguishes full, partial and no ownership, and insists that ownership is a separate choice from believing a decision is right: a leader can agree with a decision and still hold back commitment. The author then claims that leaders display a consistent pattern of ownership across decisions, so those who are tepid about some decisions rarely commit fully to any, including their own. The practical consequence is for execution, because teams read their leader's commitment exactly and mirror it in how they carry out plans, metrics and timelines. The best leaders therefore either own decisions completely or decline to finalize them, and commit to decisions from above even when they disagree. The piece closes by asserting that ownership cannot be faked and asking readers to examine their own relationship with decisions.
points: Ownership of a decision is treated as a choice distinct from agreeing with it, which the leader alone controls and cannot be compelled to make.
The author's distinctive claim is that ownership is a stable personal pattern rather than a case-by-case choice.
Any wavering in a leader's allegiance shows up in plans, metrics and timelines, and team members respond by holding back their own commitment.
The prescription is binary: own a decision fully or resist finalizing it, and commit to decisions from above even when you disagree.
quotes: Leaders develop a distinct relationship with the decisions they and others make. Decisions can be owned completely, partially, or not at all. Interestingly, the degree of ownership for a decision has little to do with the quality of the decision or whether the leader thinks it is a wise choice.
The commitment to fully embrace a decision is left entirely up to the leader. It can never be forced or compelled.

While this sounds like a decision-by-decision choice, leaders relate to decisions in generally the same way. Those who are tepid with some decisions rarely make the full commitment to own any decision, even those they make themselves.

Whenever a leader wavers to any degree in their allegiance to a decision, team execution suffers. Because a leader’s relationship with a decision is reflected in the plans, metrics, tactics, and timelines involved with implementing it, team performance is hugely impacted by it. When leaders hold their full commitment in reserve, team members respond in kind.
They choose to own decisions completely or resist making or finalizing them. When faced with decisions from above, true leaders decide to commit, even when they disagree.
In organizations, there is no such thing as faking ownership of a decision. Everyone can tell exactly where the leader stands regarding the decision. Team execution depends on it.
